title: Caitlin Colgrove, Hex: Building in Public: Why Traditional Product Launches Fail in AI

segments.text: All right, ladies and gentlemen, please
help me welcome
Kaitlyn Colgrove from Hex.
>> Hi, I'm Caitlyn. I'm the co-founder and
the CTO of Hex. And we only have a
couple minutes here today, but I really
what I want to spend some time doing is
sharing with you one of the big things
that we've learned over the past couple
years of launching products in AI. And I
was really excited to hear the data talk
a few minutes ago. For those of you who
are still here, I think you'll hear a
lot of really similar themes in what
we've been learning.
So for those of you who aren't familiar
with Hex, I'll give you a brief overview
here. I also encourage you to come stop
by our booth and get the full demo. It's
pretty cool. But basically, Hex is an
agentic AI platform for data analytics
and data scientists. And what that
means, it has the familiar agentic
experience that we all know and love
being at this conference where you can
collaborate with an agent in natural
language to answer questions with data,
but that is backed by the full power of
a complete data platform. It has a code
notebook where you can do sort of deep
analytics and deep data scientists and
SQL and Python or make visualizations.
It also has things like data modeling,
governance, security, the works. And all
of this is incorporated as tools into
the agent. So you have a richer and more
fullfeatured agentic experience.
We've been working on AI for a couple
years at this point at Hex. And in that
time, we've had the opportunity to
launch a number of really exciting
products. And you know, this started way
back in 2022. It feels like a long time
ago now when we prototyped uh on top of
GBT3, we prototyped generating SQL in
the Hex notebook. At that time, we
didn't really think it was super ready
for prime time. So we actually didn't
end up shipping it until the release of
chat GBT and GPT 3.5. That quality
improvement was big enough that we then
and we took that PC and we put it into
production for our first generative AI
feature in early 2023, which was SQL and
Python generation in Hex. But we didn't
really stop there. Right around that
time, we started learning more about
reasoning, learning more about chain of
thought. And so we sort of took that to
the next level where instead of just
generating a single SQL statement or a
single cell in hex, we actually
prototyped and then released our first
protoagentic workflow where we actually
allowed the agent to reason through more
complicated questions and generate a
series of cells in the notebook. And one
of the great things about being deeply
integrated with a data platform is that
as the platform gets better, so does the
agent. And so at the same time we were
also working on building out Hex's suite
of no code capabilities which we then
also launched an AI product to drive.
And then lastly earlier this year the
models have advanced a lot since our
first attempt at agents and we decided
to take another look at our own agent
implementation kind of from first
principles to see what we really wanted
to build. And the results of that
project we launched three weeks ago
which is very exciting. So, there's a
lot of stuff we've launched here and
we've learned a lot along the way and I
want to share a little bit of of what
we've been doing. But first, the
notebook agent. This is the launch that
we launched a couple weeks ago. If you
want to see a demo, please come by our
booth. And I'm happy to report this
launch went great. This is exactly the
type of usage graph that you want to see
whenever you have a big launch moment.
And we also got a lot of really lovely
qualitative feedback from the users who
are using our new feature. But lest you
think that I'm just up here to kind of
toot my own horn for you at 10 for 10
minutes, not all of our launches that I
just showed you on that timeline up
there. Not all of our launches have been
this successful.
This is what usage looked like for magic
analysis, our first cut at doing an
agentic workflow. We definitely had
people using it. You know, there's
there's people using it here. But I
think one thing that I've observed and I
think we've all observed in the market
is that AI features that have true
product market fit see really steep
adoption curves. So even though we had
usage, we knew there was something here
that we could be doing better. And when
we went to revisit our notebook agent,
we really wanted to think through why
this didn't see the adoption that we
hoped it would and what we could do
differently.
We also looked at launches around the
industry. you know, everything from the
sort of more traditional launch cycle
that OpenAI goes through every couple
months where they launch new models,
products like Cursor that barely launch
at all, they just constantly ship things
to big splashy launches that then fall
in their face. We started to really
unpack what was working and what wasn't
working and what would we want to do
differently with our upcoming notebook
agent launch. And there's a lot of
reasons that launches might be succeed
or fail. But we noticed a pattern
particularly in the things that we were
building and some of the outside
products. And the pattern came with how
we traditionally think about launches
and the launch life cycle for products
and where that started to break down
with AI products. So I'm sure you all
anybody who's built products here has
run a launch cycle like this. You design
an MVP, you iterate with your, you know,
closed beta with a small number of
design partners. you sort of get get it
to a point where you think it's really
great and then you have a big splashy
launch moment and you release it to
everybody. There's nothing sort of
controversial about doing this. Even if
you're a very sort of agile iterative
company, most launches and most product
development cycles look something like
this. But what we realized is as we were
doing this for more and more complex AI
features, this was starting to break
down. And again, this is where some of
those themes from the data dog talk will
come back. The first first and foremost
what we were seeing with AI features is
that it was truly impossible to evaluate
the success or the quality of a feature
based on a small cohort of data. First
of all, eval really really hard, very
hard to get a representative data set.
And even if you can do that, the actual
quality metric may be very subjective
and it may not be the thing that you're
actually measuring with your evals. I
think a really great example of this is
actually GPT5. GPT5 did really well on a
bunch of benchmarks. Like they were able
to train the model to perform really
well on those things and still there
were a number of people when they
finally released it that were really
dissatisfied with how the model
performed because there were a whole set
of things like model voice that people
weren't really factoring in and that
were a bit of a surprise when the model
actually came out. The other thing about
generative AI as we all know is it's
non-deterministic and that leads to a
much larger set of errors and edge cases
and unpredictability in the actual
feature. When you're building a
traditional feature, you can have a
relatively strong sense just from a few
users of what the quality bar is for
that feature. You can write unit tests,
you can have user acceptance tests, you
can fix bugs and find bugs. A lot of
that just by clicking through the
product. You can't do this with AI. you
have no idea what users are what users
are going to be typing in to that
product and the model could go anywhere
and so you actually need a quite big
data set to have a lot of confidence
that you are catching all of these edge
cases and then I think the other
difference that we were noticing is that
to get a really good AI feature it was
just taking a lot more iteration cycles
a lot more sort of micro iteration
cycles where okay you give it to a user
you get feedback you tune the prompt you
tune the rag things like that And so we
were being killed by these long
development cycles where you know you
would or you know comparatively long
where you would talk to a customer and
then two weeks later you'd go have
another call with them and be like we
fixed your bugs. That was just too long
in an industry where speed is
everything.
The solution to all of these we realized
is to get as much user real user data as
possible as fast as possible. And so we
decided to take a little bit of
inspiration from from cursor and instead
of sort of having a closely guarded
closed beta, we decided to do something
that we are calling building in public,
which is pretty simple. Instead of going
through this traditional launch pattern,
you just cut out the middleman. We built
our MVP and then we turned it on. And
this was really scary. We actually
turned on our notebook agent for the
vast majority of our user base weeks
after we started building it. It was
very very fast
and honestly we could not have made a
better decision. This was so
instrumental in us having both a really
high quality agent launch and also a
speed to launch. There was only two
months of iteration and we were able to
gather so much data in that time that we
had a really really polished product at
the end of it. Some things that we
learned. One, I'm sure we all know,
anybody who's worked with AI knows that
managing our context is quite hard. We
got to see a lot of what people are
doing in hex. Some of those things are
pretty crazy. Like we had someone who
was outputting thousands of lines of
HTML. And so we got really good at
managing the context that we're giving
the agent. Another thing that's less
obvious is a lot of these agents are
trained in certain environments like the
terminal, but they weren't trained for
the hex notebook as an agentic
environment. And so while by watching
users use this, we were able to make the
agent much much better at using the
specific tools to hex. For example,
leaving a clean, tidy notebook after it
sort of goes through a chain of
reasoning. And then lastly, and perhaps
most mundainely, but importantly, we
were able to get a sense of the cost
that each of these sort of agent runs
would cost us in inference. And that had
us allowed us to have a strong position
on what the economics would look like
both internally and externally when we
went into the marketing launch a few
weeks ago.
But I think most importantly, we were
able to go into the marketing launch
extremely confident that it was going to
be successful and we were able to make a
lot of noise with a lot of confidence
because we had already turned it on and
we could see in the usage data that this
product had product market fit and we
knew we were ready and we knew it was
time to launch.
Like I said, this was pretty scary.
There were a lot of things that could
have gone wrong, but after the fact, we
realized that a lot of the things we
were worried about didn't really
materialize. So, I think the first one
is just what if it's really broken and
people hate it and you lose credibility.
We were worried about this and and
candidly, the thing that we turned on
was very broken. there were a lot of
bugs in it. But early adopters for AI
know that these workflows are stepch
changing how they work and they are
ready to deal with a lot of these rough
edges and they're willing to deal with
that because they know how powerful
these these tools can be. We also
worried about our enterprise customers.
Would they be able to take advantage of
this? Would we be able to get feedback
from the enterprise? And yeah, there
were customers who didn't turn this on,
but I think you might be surprised at
how fast larger enterprises are willing
to adopt these tools. These companies
know the kind of power that AI has and
actually one of our board members in
when we were talking about this even
said that they're doing enterprise AI
evaluations in two weeks. Like
enterprises are doing that are adopting
very very quickly and so we were
actually pleasantly surprised at how
much penetration we could could get in
this in this early access period. And
then lastly, I think one thing that's
near and dear to me as a product person
and and to Hex culture is just the
overall quality bar. It really hurt to
kind of put something out there that we
didn't feel like met our standards. But
I think the thing that we kept reminding
ourselves that helped us get through it
is the only way to build something high
quality was to get as much usage data as
possible in terms of how it was actually
being used. And that was the thing that
would get us to the really high quality
feature that we ended up launching just
a few months later.
We have a few more launches coming this
year where we get to practice what we
preach and and fine-tune this process.
Um, so please stay tuned for that. If
you have any other questions, I'll be at
the booth. I'll stick around for a
couple more minutes and then please do
come by and the hex booth and I hope to
see you there. Thank you.
